power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.text: In both the twin-sibling and clinic samples the alternative Externalizing bifactor models explained greater R² in the symptoms than did the Externalizing dimension by itself (twin-sibling: Mean R² = .68 versus .50, t (252) = 6.90, p = 4.14 * 10 -11, d = 5.76; clinic: Mean R² = .72 versus .57, t (240) = 4.51, p = .00001, d = 3.86).

In contrast, there was no difference in the R² in the symptoms explained by the alternative Externalizing bifactor models from that explained by the 7 correlated fine-grained symptom factors (twin-sibling: Mean R² = .68 versus .68, t (252) = -0.14, p = .888, d = -0.10; clinic: Mean R² = .72 versus .73, t (240) = -0.39, p = .694, d = -0.28).

In contrast, there was no difference in the R² in the symptoms explained by the alternative Externalizing bifactor models from that explained by the 7 correlated fine-grained symptom factors (twin-sibling: Mean R² = .68 versus .68, t (252) = -0.14, p = .888, d = -0.10; clinic: Mean R² = .72 versus .73, t (240) = -0.39, p = .694, d = -0.28).

text.text: Externalizing is a major spectrum of the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP).
Comprehensive models of late-adolescent and adult Externalizing emphasize behavioral disinhibition, but no comprehensive models exist for youth.
We developed an elaborated model of youth Externalizing psychopathology that includes an overarching dimension and specific symptom factors.

In large diverse population-based and clinicreferred samples, we used confirmatory factor analyses of ADHD, ODD, and CD symptoms and supplemental indices to adjudicate among models of youth Externalizing.

Based on model fit, reliability, and discriminant validity, increasingly elaborated models comprising an Externalizing dimension plus seven fine-grained symptom factors outperformed simpler models containing omnibus ADHD, ODD, and CD symptom factors.
Within-disorder specific symptom factors showed distinct correlation patterns with cross-disorder symptom factors.
Results replicated across clinic and non-referred samples, with Externalizing most strongly reflecting defiant behavior.
This elaborated model is foundational for future investigations of measurement invariance, causes, correlates, and outcomes of youth Externalizing.

Externalizing psychopathology describes symptoms of DSM (American Psychiatric Association, 2013) disorders including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), oppositional defiant disorder (ODD), and conduct disorder (CD) in children and adolescents (Bezdjian et al., 2011; Lahey et al., 2004; Lahey et al., 2008), substance use disorders in older adolescents and adults (Krueger et al., 2002), and antisocial personality disorder in adults (ASPD; Krueger, Markon, Patrick, Benning, & Kramer, 2007).

Nevertheless, the importance of both levels of the psychopathology hierarchy is emphasized in data and theory driven models of psychopathology (e.g., HiTOP; Kotov et al., 2017) and in recent exploratory investigations of psychopathology broadly (Forbes et al., 2024).

text.text: The balance between these two approaches is key.

Grouping disorders with different causes, developmental courses, and responses to treatment may mask our ability to accurately operationalize psychopathology constructs and determine how they should be treated (Lahey, 2004).

text.text: Only one study to our knowledge has tested a hierarchical model with multiple DSM externalizing disorders in youth. Bezdjian and colleagues (2011) used exploratory hierarchical factor analyses to examine the covariation of symptoms of ADHD, ODD, and CD.

text.text: Their results indicated substantial covariation among symptoms of these disorders, reflected in the broad overarching externalizing dimension, and subdimensions within symptom clusters, which are reflected in lower-order factors.

At the highest levels of the hierarchy, they found support for a broad externalizing dimension that encompassed all symptoms and, at the lowest levels of the hierarchy, evidence that ADHD symptoms cluster into three separable factors of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity and that CD symptoms cluster into symptoms reflecting rulebreaking and aggression.
Notably, at the lowest levels they also observed several instances of cross-disorder loadings in which items also loaded onto factors other than the disorder they represent.
For example, some CD symptoms loaded on the ODD dimension and some hyperactivity items loaded on the CD dimension.
Herein we propose an elaborated model of externalizing psychopathology in youth.
By elaborated, we mean a model that encompasses both a general Externalizing dimension as well as several fine-grained specific symptom factors.
This model can best capture both the commonality among and uniqueness of different aspects of externalizing psychopathology.

To test this model, we analyze symptom-level data, given that symptoms are more granular than diagnoses or symptom dimensions, thus provide more information which should better allow meaningful distinctions among factors to emerge (Levin-Aspenson, 2023; Waldman and Poore, 2023).

text.text: Despite the desirability of these two properties of model elaboration and granularity, few studies have embodied them.
As shown in Supplementary Table 1, few representative recent studies of Externalizing psychopathology have included symptom-level data that encompass the disorders ADHD, ODD, and CD.

text.text: We explore the utility of several approaches for adjudicating among alternative models of externalizing psychopathology in youth using confirmatory factor analyses and relevant supplemental indices.

Specifically, we compared 1) models with only a broad Externalizing dimension or only specific symptom factors to models that include both simultaneously and 2) models with disorder-level symptom factors (i.e., ADHD, ODD, and CD) to models with more fine-grained symptom factors that represent meaningful heterogeneity within disorders (e.g., inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity separately within ADHD).
To make these comparisons and to help adjudicate among alternative models we used a combination of conventional fit indices and alternative indices.

The latter reflect important model characteristics such as differences across models in: 1. the percent of variance explained in individual symptoms by the factors in the model; and 2. the magnitude of Externalizing and specific factor loadings, their precision (standard errors, or SEs), and their variability (standard deviations, or SDs).

We conducted these analyses separately in two large samples of youth, a population representative sample of twins and their siblings and a clinic-referred sample, which allowed us to examine the replicability of our findings on the structure of externalizing psychopathology as well as its components (e.g., factor loadings' magnitudes and their precision and variability).

We hypothesized that more elaborated models (i.e., those with a broad Externalizing dimension as well as fine-grained symptom factors) would better represent externalizing psychopathology in youth than simpler models.

This should aid in identifying the most comprehensive and valid operationalization of youth externalizing psychopathology useful for subsequent studies of its etiology, course, correlates, and treatment.

We used three metrics to evaluate the performance of each model: 1) traditional goodness-of-fit indices, 2) the variance explained in each symptom by their respective factors, and 3) information about the standardized factor loadings, including their magnitude (i.e., means), precision (i.e., standard errors [SEs]), and variability (i.e., standard deviations [SDs], and contrasted these across models.

We used these supplemental indices as they can aid in adjudicating among competing models that show very similar model fit, or when fit indices may be biased for certain models (e.g., due to overfitting or to the model's fit propensity (Bonifay & Cai, 2017; Preacher, 2006).

text.text: First, for goodness-of-fit indices, which indicate the discrepancy between the variance/covariance matrix implied by the model and the variance/covariance matrix in the observed data, we report the c 2 statistic and its associated degrees of freedom, Comparative Fit Index (CFI), Tucker-Lewis index (TLI), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) and its 95% confidence interval, and weighted root mean square residual (WRMR).
Each individual fit index has its own strengths and limitations, and no consensus has been reached regarding the superiority of one over the other (Loehlin & Beaujean, 2017).

text.text: We used ANOVAs with targeted a priori orthogonal contrasts to test differences in these alternative indices across bifactor models that include the Externalizing dimension and specific symptom factors.

Specifically, these contrasts test differences in models that include: 1. the 7 fine-grained specific symptom factors versus the 3 ADHD, ODD, and CD symptom factors, and 2. orthogonal versus correlated specific factors.
These contrasts are intended to test our hypotheses about the importance of increasing model elaboration for the validity of alternative models of youth Externalizing.
Effect sizes for these indices are presented alongside all statistical hypothesis tests.
Thirteen item-level CFAs with increasing complexity were specified to evaluate and contrast alternative models of the underlying structure of youth externalizing psychopathology.
Externalizing was parameterized using both a bifactor and a higher-order factor framework.

Bifactor models included a general Externalizing dimension onto which all symptoms load, and specific symptom factors that were orthogonal to the externalizing dimension, onto which only some symptoms load.
Thus, the Externalizing dimension captures the covariance among all symptoms, whereas the specific factors capture covariance that is unique to that construct (e.g. inattention).
The higher-order model differs by having all specific symptom factors load on the Externalizing dimension.
We also tested modified versions of these models in which residual correlations were included among all or some of the specific factors, as described below.

text.text: Methodologically, we demonstrated the value of recently proposed (Waldman et al., 2023) simple descriptive statistical indices as adjuncts to using model fit for adjudicating among alternative structural models of psychopathology.
text.formatted: Methodologically, we demonstrated the value of recently proposed <ref type="bibr">(Waldman et al., 2023)</ref> simple descriptive statistical indices as adjuncts to using model fit for adjudicating among alternative structural models of psychopathology.

text.text: The majority of applied researchers still rely exclusively on conventional fit indices for adjudicating among rival structural models of psychopathology despite their shortcomings.
Herein we demonstrate the value of simple alternative indices that resolved important differences among competing models even when they had similar fit indices.

Second, we demonstrated that the more elaborated the model, the more variance in the symptom indicators is attributable to the fine-grained specific symptom factors while the variance attributable to the general Externalizing dimension stays quite constant.
This means that the specific factors are better targets for investigating causes, correlates, and outcomes in more elaborated models than in simpler models of youth externalizing.

Third, we demonstrated a high degree of replication of our findings across multiple distinct criteria (i.e., model fit; the magnitude, precision, and variability of standardized factor loadings; discriminant validity) between non-referred and clinically-referred samples.
There also are several noteworthy specific findings from this study.
First, more elaborated models of Externalizing fit best, but other less complex models fit well and thus could be considered as reasonable contenders.
Adjudicating among these models relied on alternative indices in addition to conventional model fit indices, as discussed below.
Second, the strongest indicator of youth Externalizing appears to be Defiant Behavior based on loadings of the 7 finegrained symptom factors on the higher-order Externalizing factor.

Third, there was strong replication between the clinic and twin-sibling samples, given the high correlation of symptoms' factor loadings on the Externalizing dimension and the specific symptom factors.

This held for all bifactor models of Externalizing except the Externalizing + correlated ADHD, ODD, and CD factors model, which despite showing good model fit had many problematic model features, likely due to overfitting.
Externalizing factor loadings were higher in the clinic than the twinsibling sample, despite similar levels of specific factor loadings across the two samples.
This may reflect the greater level of cohesiveness of indicators of overall Externalizing in clinical relative to non-clinical populations.
Fourth, several alternative indices favored more versus less elaborated models of youth Externalizing, despite somewhat similar fit.

Increased model elaboration was associated with a linear increase in the variance explained in symptoms by the specific factors -but not by the Externalizing dimension -and a greater balance in the variance explained by the specific factors relative to the Externalizing dimension.

While the magnitude of Externalizing dimension loadings did not differ across models, specific factor loadings were higher in more elaborated models, and both sets of factor loadings were more homogenous and more precisely estimated in more elaborated models.

Fifth, there were important differences in the specific symptom factors within DSM disorders in their correlations with the fine-grained specific symptom factors within the other disorders, suggesting unique profiles of comorbidity for each specific symptom factor.
Relative to Inattention, Impulsivity and Hyperactivity showed higher correlations with Irritability (in the clinic sample), Defiant Behavior, and Aggression.
Relative to Irritability, Defiant Behavior showed higher correlations with Impulsivity, Hyperactivity, and Aggression in the twin sample and with rule Breaking in both samples.

Finally, relative to Rule Breaking, Aggression showed higher correlations with Impulsivity, Hyperactivity (in the clinic sample), Irritability, and Defiant Behavior, whereas Rule Breaking showed a higher correlation with Inattention (in the twin sample).
Pending further replication, these differences in comorbidity could have both research and clinical implications.

Models of Externalizing in the extant literature -whether at the phenotypic (Krueger et al., 2021a; Lahey et al., 2004 Lahey et al., , 2008) ) or etiological level (Karlsson Linnér, Mallard, Barr, Sanchez-Roige, Dick, et al., 2021; Lahey et al., 2011; Waldman et al., 2016) -have exclusively or primarily focused on the broad Externalizing dimension at the expense of the narrower specific or lower-order factors (cf. (Barr et al., 2022)).

text.text: Herein, we showed how this focus may be myopic.
In this study we integrated DSM symptoms and their fine-grained factors into an elaborated model of youth Externalizing psychopathology.
An elaborated model of youth Externalizing as specified herein has a number of advantages.
First, it includes and integrates disparate specific fine-grained symptom factors that have appeared largely in isolation in the extant child psychopathology literature.

While researchers have delineated specific symptom factors within ADHD (Lahey et al., 1994; Nikolas & Burt, 2010), ODD (Burke et al., 2014; Rowe et al., 2010; Stringaris & Goodman, 2009; Waldman et al., 2021), and CD (Burt, 2009 (Burt, , 2012;; Lahey et al., 1998; Nock et al., 2006; Tackett et al., 2003 Tackett et al., , 2005)), as well as across these disorders (Burt et al., 2001; Dick et al., 2005; Lahey et al., 2004 Lahey et al., , 2008 Lahey et al., , 2011;; Olino et al., 2014 Olino et al., , 2018;; Waldman et al., 2001 Waldman et al., , 2016;; Watts, Poore, & Waldman, 2019), these factors have not previously been integrated into a comprehensive model that also includes an overarching Externalizing dimension.

text.text: Hierarchical dimensional models of psychopathology typically have focused on higher-order dimensions, such as Externalizing, while neglecting lower-order specific factors.
Our elaborated model rectifies this by encompassing both an overarching Externalizing dimension and 7 fine-grained specific symptom factors without sacrificing one for the other.

The advantages of this more elaborated model were demonstrated by better fit, increased explained variance in individual symptoms, more balanced contributions of the Externalizing dimension and specific factors to symptoms' explained variance, better measurement precision and lower variability in the loadings of symptoms on their factors, the replication of these results across both non-referred and clinically-referred samples, and differentiated patterns of comorbidity among the specific factors.

Relatedly, it was only in the more elaborated models that an appreciable amount of variance in the individual symptoms was accounted for by the finegrained specific factors, which is important for them to be useful as predictors of important criteria and as outcomes of relevant risk factors.
Such nuanced findings would be missed in models that include only omnibus ADHD, ODD, and CD symptom dimensions (Perlstein et al., 2024; Vize et al., 2023).

In addition to the importance of model elaboration, we contend that more granular indicators of psychopathology -individual symptoms in the present case -allow for more reliable and valid characterizations of both higher-and lower-order psychopathology factors relative to diagnoses or symptom dimensions (Forbes et al., 2023; Levin-Aspenson, 2023).

text.text: Indeed, it is difficult to imagine that our findings supporting the importance of increased model elaboration would have emerged without the use of symptom-level indicators, given the greater information they provide.

Across both samples, the bifactor and higher-order models containing an Externalizing dimension plus 7 fine-grained specific symptom factors with within-disorder correlated residuals fit best, equivalent to the fit of a model with 7 correlated symptom factors.

Less elaborated models of Externalizing with 3 specific symptom factors corresponding to ADHD, ODD, and CD fit a bit worse, whereas models with an Externalizing dimension only or 3 or 7 orthogonal symptom factors alone fit poorly.

These results suggest that the best use of fit indices may not be to declare that one model is victorious over all others, but rather to exclude certain models as untenable and include others as viable contenders (Waldman et al., 2023).

text.text: Rather than being in opposition to each other, some of the alternative contender models may have different uses.
As an example, bifactor and higher-order models often are very difficult to discriminate based on model fit (Markon, 2019; Mulaik & Quartetti, 1997).

text.text: Our findings herein suggest that the higherorder model was particularly useful in showing that Externalizing most strongly reflected the Defiant Behavior symptom domain, whereas the bifactor model was particularly useful for investigating the measurement properties of the Externalizing dimension and specific symptom factors.

We suspect that the bifactor model also will be more useful in external validity analyses of associations of the Externalizing dimension and 7 fine-grained specific symptom factors with relevant causes, correlates, and outcomes.

Given that conventional fit indices only take one so far in model adjudication, herein we showed the incremental importance of using supplemental indices of model reliability and validity, rather than relying only on model fit as is the norm in studies of the structure of psychopathology.

Specifically, we showed that one could meaningfully differentiate among alternative bifactor models of externalizing based on: 1. the balance of variance explained in individual symptoms by the specific symptom factors versus the Externalizing dimension, 2. the magnitude, variability, and (to a lesser extent) precision of loadings on the specific symptom factors and Externalizing dimension, 3. replication of results across non-referred and clinicreferred samples, and 4. differences in the comorbidity patterns of specific symptom factors within DSM disorders.
These findings highlight the importance of using alternative indices to augment conventional fit indices in adjudicating among alternative models of psychopathology (Waldman et al., 2023).

text.text: Our study had several limitations that should be redressed in future research.
First, we had to exclude several conduct disorder symptoms due to low endorsement rates, which may not have been the case if we had a much larger sample.
While omission of these symptoms may not have affected the structure of Externalizing, it may have limited our ability to precisely measure and effectively cover Externalizing at the higher extreme.
Second, our data were limited to parent report.

Future research should examine the structure, reliability, replicability, measurement, and external validity of Externalizing using data from multiple sources, including teachers and the youth themselves (once they reach late childhood).

One caveat regarding this recommendation is that children have been shown not to be optimal informants for externalizing psychopathology, particularly ADHD and ODD symptoms (Jensen et al., 1999; Loeber et al., 1990 Loeber et al., , 1991)).

text.text: Third, we tested alternative models of Externalizing across a wide age range.

Future studies using larger samples should examine developmental similarities and differences in this elaborated model and measurement and structural invariance of the Externalizing dimension and the fine-grained specific symptom factors across age.
There are also several profitable future directions that follow from the research we present herein.
First, our findings should be replicated in both large non-referred population-based and clinic-referred samples.
This should be achievable given the availability of large samples containing data on youth externalizing symptoms assessed using different measures.

Such research will help in evaluating the replicability and validity of our best-fitting models, as well as the importance of a model that includes both an Externalizing dimension and more fine-grained symptom factors.

Second, related to the point above, our elaborated model of youth externalizing should be extended to examine measurement and structural invariance in other samples that include participants of different racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic backgrounds.
Longitudinal studies also should be conducted to examine phenotypic and etiologic continuities and changes in the Externalizing dimension and the fine-grained symptom factors across development.
Third, our results suggested unique profiles of comorbidity for each specific symptom factor.
Pending further replication, these differences in comorbidity could have both important research and clinical implications.

For example, these comorbidity profiles may be useful in guiding the search for genetic and environmental risk factors that are unique to each symptom factor or common across subsets of those factors.

Similarly, these profiles could be used to find preventive and therapeutic interventions specifically tailored to particular symptom factors or sets thereof which may help lay the groundwork for more personalized interventions.

Future research should focus on extending the discriminant validity findings we presented herein by extensively examining the associations of both the Externalizing dimension and the fine-grained specific symptom factors with external validators across various domains.

These may include constructs in the domains of relevant behavioral, personality, and neurocognitive correlates (e.g., Poore & Waldman, 2025), as well as causes such as genetic and environmental risk factors (e.g., Hicks et al., 2004; Waldman & Poore, 2023), correlates (e.g., neurocognitive underpinnings), and outcomes (e.g., various aspects of adult adjustment).

Figures 4a and 4b about here DiscussionThere are several novel contributions of this study which represent important advances over the extant literature on both substantive and methodological fronts.

Substantively, to our knowledge this represents the first comprehensive HiTOP-inspired dimensional model of youth Externalizing psychopathology that includes both an overarching general Externalizing dimension as well as fine-grained specific symptom factors.

As such, it synthesizes and extends the extant literature on the specific symptom factors which heretofore have almost exclusively been studied separately within traditional DSM youth disruptive disorders (i.e., ADHD, ODD, and CD).
Second, this model replicated across both samples of clinically-referred youth and non-referred twins and siblings.
This suggests the clinical utility of this model for assessing externalizing psychopathology both in clinically-referred populations and as a screening tool in non-referred populations.

Third, as a validator we demonstrated unique patterns of correlations of each fine-grained specific factor with the other externalizing factors, despite being moderately-to-highly correlated within the traditional DSM diagnostic categories.

This elaborated model of Externalizing thus lays the foundation for investigations of: a. measurement and structural invariance across age / development, sex, and race and ethnicity; and b. different causes (e.g., genetic and environmental risk factors) and outcomes (e.g., various aspects of adjustment and life outcomes) of the Externalizing dimension as well as the fine-grained specific symptom factors.
